subject: science
name: Describing Motion Around Us
summary: Motion is always described from a reference point. We use position, distance and displacement to say where something is and how far it has gone; speed, velocity and acceleration to say how fast and how that is changing; graphs to picture motion; the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion to calculate it; and uniform circular motion to see that constant speed can still mean acceleration.

topics.title: Reference point, position and types of motion
topics.summary: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to a reference point; along a straight line, position is given as a + or − distance from that reference point.
topics.simple: Whether something is moving depends on what you compare it with. A passenger sitting in a train is at rest compared to the seat, but moving compared to the platform. We pick a **reference point** (origin) and say how far and in which direction an object is from it — that's its **position**.
topics.explain:
**Reference point (origin):** a fixed point from which we measure position. Motion is **relative** — the same object can be at rest for one observer and moving for another.

An object is **in motion** if its position changes with time relative to the reference point; otherwise it is **at rest**.

**Position along a straight line:** choose the origin O and a positive direction (say east or right).
- A point 20 m to the right of O has position **+20 m**
- A point 15 m to the left has position **−15 m**
The sign tells the **direction**, and the number tells the **distance from O**.

**Uniform motion:** an object covers **equal distances in equal intervals of time**, however small the intervals — e.g. a car moving steadily at 60 km/h on a straight highway.
**Non-uniform motion:** unequal distances in equal time intervals — e.g. a bus in city traffic, a ball rolling down a slope.

**Motion in more than one dimension:**
- **1-D (straight line):** a train on a straight track — one number (with sign) gives position.
- **2-D (in a plane):** a carrom striker, a car on a flat city map — two numbers (like x and y) are needed.
- **3-D (in space):** a flying bird or drone — three numbers (x, y, z) are needed.
In this chapter we mostly study straight-line motion; ideas like displacement and velocity then extend to 2-D and 3-D using directions.
topics.example: From your school gate (origin, east = +), your house is at +800 m and the bus stop is at −300 m. The house is 800 m east; the bus stop is 300 m west.
keyPoints: Motion is relative to a reference point
Position = signed distance from origin along a line (+ / −)
Uniform motion: equal distances in equal time intervals
Non-uniform motion: unequal distances in equal time intervals
1-D needs one number, 2-D two, 3-D three to fix position

topics.title: Distance and displacement
topics.summary: Distance is the total length of the path travelled (a scalar, never negative); displacement is the shortest straight-line change in position from start to finish, with direction (a vector, can be zero or negative).
topics.simple: **Distance** is how much ground you actually covered. **Displacement** is how far you ended up from where you started, in a straight line, with a direction. If you walk around a park and come back to the gate, your distance is the whole walk, but your displacement is zero.
topics.explain:
**Distance:** the total length of the actual path covered.
- Has only size (magnitude) → a **scalar**
- Always positive (or zero if you don't move)

**Displacement:** the change in position, i.e. the shortest straight-line distance from the initial position to the final position, **with direction**.
- Has size and direction → a **vector**
- Along a line: **displacement = final position − initial position**
- Can be positive, negative or **zero**

**Key facts:**
- Magnitude of displacement ≤ distance
- They are equal only when the object moves in one straight line without turning back
- If an object returns to its starting point, displacement = 0 but distance ≠ 0

**SI unit** of both: metre (m).

**Scalars and vectors:**
- **Scalar:** only magnitude — distance, speed, time, mass
- **Vector:** magnitude and direction — displacement, velocity, acceleration

**Worked example (clock hand):** the minute hand of a clock is 10 cm long. Find its tip's distance and displacement in 30 minutes.
- In 30 min the tip goes from 12 to 6 — half a circle.
- **Displacement** = straight line from 12 to 6 = diameter = 2 × 10 = **20 cm**
- **Distance** = half the circumference = πr = (22/7) × 10 ≈ **31.43 cm**
- Distance is larger than displacement, as expected.
topics.example: A person walks 40 m east, then 10 m west. Distance = 40 + 10 = 50 m. Final position = +30 m, so displacement = 30 m east.
keyPoints: Distance = total path length; scalar; never negative
Displacement = final − initial position; vector; can be zero or negative
Clock minute hand (10 cm) in 30 min: displacement 20 cm, distance ≈ 31.43 cm

topics.title: Speed and velocity
topics.summary: Speed = distance ÷ time (scalar); velocity = displacement ÷ time (vector). Average speed is over a whole trip, instantaneous speed is at one moment; for uniform acceleration, average velocity = (u + v)/2.
topics.simple: **Speed** tells how fast something moves. **Velocity** tells how fast *and in which direction*. A car's speedometer shows its speed at that instant. If you divide the total distance of a trip by the total time, you get the average speed.
topics.explain:
**Speed** = distance travelled ÷ time taken
- A **scalar**; SI unit **m/s** (also km/h)
- **Average speed** = total distance ÷ total time
- **Instantaneous speed** = speed at a particular moment — what a speedometer shows

**Velocity** = displacement ÷ time taken
- A **vector** (speed in a given direction); SI unit m/s
- Velocity changes if the **speed changes**, the **direction changes**, or both
- **Average velocity** = total displacement ÷ total time

**Average velocity for uniform acceleration:** when velocity changes at a steady rate from initial velocity u to final velocity v,
**v_av = (u + v) / 2**

**Unit conversion:**
- km/h → m/s: multiply by **5/18** (because 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s)
- m/s → km/h: multiply by **18/5**
- 36 km/h = 10 m/s; 54 km/h = 15 m/s; 72 km/h = 20 m/s

**Why average speed and average velocity can differ:** on a round trip, average velocity is zero (displacement is zero) but average speed is not.
topics.deep: Average speed is NOT the average of two speeds when the times are different. If you go 60 km at 30 km/h (2 h) and return 60 km at 60 km/h (1 h), average speed = 120 km ÷ 3 h = 40 km/h, not 45 km/h.
topics.example:
A student cycles 3 km to school in 15 min and back the same way in 15 min.
- Total distance = 6 km, total time = 0.5 h
- Average speed = 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12 km/h
- Displacement = 0, so average velocity = 0
keyPoints: Round trip: average velocity = 0, average speed ≠ 0

topics.title: Acceleration
topics.summary: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = (v − u)/t, measured in m/s²; it can be uniform or non-uniform, and negative acceleration (retardation) means slowing down.
topics.simple: **Acceleration** tells how quickly velocity changes. When a bike speeds up, it accelerates. When it brakes and slows down, it has **negative acceleration** (also called **retardation** or deceleration). If velocity changes by the same amount every second, the acceleration is **uniform**.
topics.explain:
**Acceleration** = change in velocity ÷ time taken
**a = (v − u) / t**
where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, t = time.
- A **vector**; SI unit **m/s²** (metre per second per second)
- a = 2 m/s² means the velocity increases by 2 m/s every second

**Types:**
- **Positive acceleration:** velocity increasing in the direction of motion (a bus pulling away from a stop)
- **Negative acceleration / retardation:** velocity decreasing (a car braking at a red light). a has a minus sign.
- **Uniform acceleration:** velocity changes by **equal amounts in equal time intervals** — e.g. a stone falling freely (ignoring air)
- **Non-uniform acceleration:** velocity changes by unequal amounts in equal time intervals — e.g. a car in stop-and-go traffic
- **Zero acceleration:** constant velocity (same speed in the same direction)

**Acceleration without speeding up:** since velocity includes direction, an object changing direction at constant speed is also accelerating (see circular motion).

**Worked example (bike):** a bike's speed rises from 54 km/h to 72 km/h in 2 s. Find its acceleration.
- u = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s; v = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s; t = 2 s
- a = (v − u)/t = (20 − 15)/2 = **2.5 m/s²**
topics.example:
A car moving at 20 m/s brakes and stops in 5 s.
- a = (0 − 20)/5 = −4 m/s²
- The minus sign shows retardation of 4 m/s².
keyPoints: Uniform: equal change in velocity in equal time
Non-uniform: unequal change in equal time
Always convert km/h to m/s before calculating

topics.title: Position-time and velocity-time graphs
topics.summary: The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity; the slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and the area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
topics.simple: Graphs let us 'see' motion. On a **position-time graph**, a steeper line means faster motion. On a **velocity-time graph**, the steepness shows acceleration, and the area under the line tells you how far the object moved.
topics.explain:
**Position-time (x–t) graph** — time on the x-axis, position on the y-axis.
- **Slope = velocity** (change in position ÷ change in time)
- Horizontal line → object at rest (velocity 0)
- Straight sloping line → **uniform** velocity; steeper = faster
- Line sloping downward → moving in the negative direction
- Curved line → velocity changing (non-uniform motion / acceleration)

**Velocity-time (v–t) graph** — time on the x-axis, velocity on the y-axis.
- **Slope = acceleration** (change in velocity ÷ change in time)
- Horizontal line → constant velocity (acceleration 0)
- Straight line sloping up → uniform acceleration
- Straight line sloping down → uniform retardation
- Curved line → non-uniform acceleration
- **Area under the v–t graph = displacement** (distance, if the motion is in one direction)

**Finding area:** break the region into rectangles and triangles.
- Rectangle: length × breadth
- Triangle: ½ × base × height

The equations of motion can be derived from the v–t graph: the slope gives v = u + at, and the area (rectangle + triangle) gives s = ut + ½at².
topics.example:
A scooter starts from rest and its velocity rises steadily to 10 m/s in 5 s.
- Slope = (10 − 0)/5 = 2 m/s² → acceleration
- Area under v–t = triangle = ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m → displacement
keyPoints: Curved graph = changing velocity (x–t) or changing acceleration (v–t)

topics.title: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
topics.summary: For constant acceleration along a straight line: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², and v² − u² = 2as.
topics.simple: When acceleration stays constant, three equations connect five quantities: starting velocity (u), final velocity (v), acceleration (a), time (t) and displacement (s). If you know any three, you can find the other two.
topics.explain:
These equations apply **only when acceleration is uniform** (constant) and the motion is along a straight line.

**Symbols:** u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, s = displacement.

1. **v = u + at** (velocity–time relation)
2. **s = ut + ½at²** (position–time relation)
3. **v² − u² = 2as** (position–velocity relation)

Also useful: **s = v_av × t = ((u + v)/2) × t**

**Tips:**
- 'Starts from rest' → u = 0; 'comes to rest / stops' → v = 0
- Retardation → put a as negative
- Convert all units to m, s, m/s, m/s² first
- Pick the equation that doesn't contain the quantity you don't know and don't need

**Worked example 1 (car braking):** a car brakes with a = −4 m/s² and stops in 3 s. Find its initial speed and stopping distance.
- v = u + at → 0 = u + (−4)(3) → **u = 12 m/s**
- s = ut + ½at² = 12 × 3 + ½ × (−4) × 3² = 36 − 18 = **18 m**
- Check: v² − u² = 2as → 0 − 144 = 2(−4)s → s = 18 m ✓

**Worked example 2 (bike):** 54 km/h (15 m/s) to 72 km/h (20 m/s) in 2 s, a = 2.5 m/s². Distance covered?
- s = ut + ½at² = 15 × 2 + ½ × 2.5 × 2² = 30 + 5 = **35 m**
- Check: s = ((15 + 20)/2) × 2 = 17.5 × 2 = 35 m ✓
topics.example: A train starts from rest with acceleration 0.5 m/s². After 20 s: v = 0 + 0.5 × 20 = 10 m/s, and s = ½ × 0.5 × 20² = 100 m.
keyPoints: From rest: u = 0; stops: v = 0; braking: a negative
Car at −4 m/s² stopping in 3 s: u = 12 m/s, s = 18 m

topics.title: Uniform circular motion
topics.summary: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has speed v = 2πr/T, but its velocity keeps changing direction (along the tangent), so it is accelerated.
topics.simple: When something goes round a circle at a steady speed, its **speed** stays the same but its **direction** changes every moment. Since velocity includes direction, the velocity is changing — so the object is **accelerating**, even though it isn't speeding up.
topics.explain:
**Uniform circular motion:** motion of an object along a circular path at **constant speed**.

**Speed:** in one round (time period T), the object covers the circumference 2πr.
**v = 2πr / T**
where r = radius of the circle and T = time for one full round.

**Why it is accelerated motion:**
- At every point, the direction of motion is along the **tangent** to the circle at that point.
- As the object moves, this tangent direction keeps changing.
- So **velocity changes** (direction changes) even though **speed is constant**.
- A change in velocity means **acceleration**. Hence uniform circular motion is an **accelerated motion**.

**Proof you can see:** if you whirl a stone tied to a string and let go, the stone flies off in a straight line along the **tangent** at the point of release — showing the direction it was moving at that instant.

**Examples:**
- The Moon going around the Earth, and the Earth around the Sun (nearly circular)
- The tip of a clock's second hand
- A cyclist on a circular track at steady speed
- A point on a ceiling fan blade
topics.example:
An athlete runs one round of a circular track of radius 35 m in 44 s.
- Circumference = 2 × (22/7) × 35 = 220 m
- v = 2πr/T = 220 ÷ 44 = 5 m/s
- After one full round, displacement = 0 and average velocity = 0, though average speed is 5 m/s.
keyPoints: Uniform circular motion: constant speed on a circle
Direction of motion is along the tangent
Velocity changes → it is accelerated motion
A released stone flies off along the tangent

keyConcepts.meaning: A fixed point (origin) from which the position of an object is measured; motion is always described relative to it.
Total length of the path travelled; a scalar that is never negative.
Shortest straight-line change in position from start to end, with direction; a vector that can be zero or negative.
A quantity with only magnitude, e.g. distance, speed, time, mass.
A quantity with magnitude and direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, acceleration.
Distance travelled per unit time; average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Speed at a particular instant, as shown by a speedometer.
Displacement per unit time; speed in a given direction.
Rate of change of velocity, a = (v − u)/t, in m/s².
Negative acceleration; the object is slowing down.
Equal distances covered in equal intervals of time.
Motion in a circle at constant speed; velocity changes direction, so it is accelerated.

formulas: Speed = distance ÷ time; average speed = total distance ÷ total time
Displacement (along a line) = final position − initial position
a = (v − u)/t (u initial velocity, v final velocity, t time)
v = 2πr/T (uniform circular motion; r radius, T time for one round)
commonMistakes: Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s (× 5/18) before using the equations of motion.
Taking displacement equal to distance even when the path curves or turns back.
Not putting a minus sign on acceleration when an object is slowing down.
Thinking an object moving at constant speed cannot be accelerating — in circular motion the direction changes, so it accelerates.
Using v = u + at and the other equations when acceleration is not uniform.
Averaging two speeds directly ((30 + 60)/2) for a trip — average speed is total distance ÷ total time.
Reading the slope of a position-time graph as acceleration — it is velocity; the slope of a v–t graph is acceleration.

faqs.q: What is the difference between distance and displacement?
faqs.a: **Distance** is the total length of the path covered — a scalar, always positive. **Displacement** is the straight-line change in position from start to finish, with direction — a vector that can be zero or negative. If you run one full lap of a track, distance = one lap, displacement = 0.

faqs.q: Can an object have constant speed but still be accelerating?
faqs.a: Yes. In **uniform circular motion**, speed stays the same but the direction of motion keeps changing along the tangent. Since velocity includes direction, velocity changes — and any change in velocity is acceleration.

faqs.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph tell us?
faqs.a: The **area under a v–t graph gives the displacement**. For example, if velocity rises steadily from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s, the area is a triangle: ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m. (The slope of the same graph gives acceleration.)

faqs.q: What is the difference between speed and velocity?
faqs.a: **Speed** = distance ÷ time and has no direction (scalar). **Velocity** = displacement ÷ time and includes direction (vector). A car going round a roundabout at a steady 20 km/h has constant speed but changing velocity.

faqs.q: How do I choose which equation of motion to use?
faqs.a:
List what you know and what you want among u, v, a, t, s. Choose the equation that contains the unknown you want and only quantities you know:
- No s → v = u + at
- No v → s = ut + ½at²
- No t → v² − u² = 2as
Remember: from rest u = 0, stops v = 0, slowing down a is negative.

quiz.q: A person walks 30 m east and then 10 m west. What is the displacement?
quiz.explain: Final position = +30 − 10 = +20 m, i.e. 20 m east. (Distance = 40 m.)

quiz.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
quiz.explain: Velocity has both magnitude and direction; the others are scalars.

quiz.q: The minute hand of a clock is 10 cm long. What is the displacement of its tip in 30 minutes?
quiz.explain: In 30 min the tip moves from 12 to 6: displacement = diameter = 20 cm. The distance is πr ≈ 31.43 cm.

quiz.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s. Its average velocity is:
quiz.explain: For uniform acceleration, v_av = (u + v)/2 = (10 + 30)/2 = 20 m/s.

quiz.q: A bike speeds up from 54 km/h to 72 km/h in 2 s. Its acceleration is:
An object whose velocity decreases with time has:
quiz.explain: Slowing down means negative acceleration, also called retardation.

quiz.q: The slope of a position-time graph gives:
quiz.explain: Change in position ÷ change in time = velocity. The slope of a v–t graph gives acceleration.

quiz.q: On a v–t graph, velocity rises steadily from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s. The displacement in this time is:
quiz.explain: Area under the graph = ½ × 5 × 10 = 25 m.

quiz.q: A car brakes with acceleration −4 m/s² and stops in 3 s. How far does it travel while braking?
quiz.explain: 0 = u − 4×3 gives u = 12 m/s. s = ut + ½at² = 36 − 18 = 18 m.

quiz.q: Which equation of motion does NOT contain time t?
quiz.explain: v² − u² = 2as links velocities, acceleration and displacement without time.

quiz.q: Why is uniform circular motion called accelerated motion?
options: Because the direction of velocity keeps changing
Because the object stops at each point
quiz.explain: Speed is constant, but the direction (along the tangent) changes continuously, so velocity changes.
